title: Long-term (>7-year) neurodevelopmental safety assessment of genetically modified (Cry1Ab/Cry2Aj and EPSPS) maize in cynomolgus monkeys: A multimodal MRI study across two generations.
abstract: The safety of genetically modified (GM) crops remains a critical topic of public and scientific concern. Despite widespread cultivation, the chronic and multigenerational neurodevelopmental toxicity of GM crops remains inadequately assessed. To address this issue, the present study evaluated the long-term safety of GM maize through a multiyear (>7 years) dietary assessment in cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis) across two generations (F0 and F1). Unlike previous studies, this work uniquely integrates three key strengths: a prolonged exposure period, inclusion of two generations, and the application of advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to assess both structural and functional brain changes. Animals were fed either a dual-transgenic maize (expressing Cry1Ab/Cry2Aj and EPSPS), its non-GM isogenic counterpart, or a conventional diet. Multimodal MRI was employed to evaluate brain morphology and resting-state function. Both voxel-wise whole-brain analyses and region-of-interest (ROI) analyses of four predefined neurotoxicity-sensitive regions (orbitofrontal cortex, hippocampus, striatum, and pallidum) were performed. Statistical models controlled for age and sex, with multiple comparison corrections applied. No significant differences were observed in brain morphological or resting-state functional metrics in either whole-brain or ROI analyses across groups in both generations, even under uncorrected thresholds (p < 0.001). These findings provide robust, nonhuman primate-based evidence that long-term, two-generational dietary exposure to dual-transgenic maize does not induce measurable or systematic alterations in brain structure or function. This study addresses a critical gap by providing comprehensive, high-resolution neuroimaging evidence to support the neurodevelopmental safety of GM maize.
